title: Terms of Recovery
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 3 of 40
content:
Madam Pomfrey arrived in the dungeon at nine the next morning carrying a potion the color of old brass and the expression of a woman prepared to commit violence in the name of medicine.

Snape saw her from across the room and immediately turned toward the storeroom.

“Oh, no you don't,” she said.

He stopped.

I became extremely interested in counting jars of powdered bicorn horn.

“Your dose was due at eight.”

“I was occupied.”

“You were hiding.”

“I do not hide from you, Poppy.”

“You have been hiding from me since 1982.”

“That is a grotesque exaggeration.”

“Drink.”

She held out the goblet.

Snape looked at it as though it contained moral failure.

“Your bedside manner remains an inspiration.”

“And yours put three generations of children off Potions. Drink.”

I bit the inside of my cheek.

His eyes snapped toward me.

“Something amusing?”

“Not remotely.”

“Liar.”

“Patient,” Pomfrey corrected. “Drink.”

He drank.

The potion smelled of valerian, iron, and something medicinally sour. Snape swallowed without flinching until the last mouthful, when his hand tightened around the cup.

Pomfrey took it from him.

“Sit.”

“I am not a dog.”

“No dog has ever argued with me this much.”

He sat.

She examined the scar at his throat with a wand tip glowing pale blue. I looked away, not because the wound was unpleasant but because Snape had gone very still. Privacy could be physical even in a room with no walls between us.

“Better,” Pomfrey said. “Still too much inflammation. Are you using the salve?”

“Yes.”

“He's lying,” I said.

The silence was immediate.

Snape turned his head very slowly.

Pomfrey looked delighted.

“How do you know?” she asked.

“The jar hasn't moved from the shelf since I arrived.”

Snape's stare could have stripped varnish.

“I use my own formulation.”

“Where?”

His jaw worked.

Pomfrey folded her arms.

He pointed toward his private office.

“Bring it,” she said to me.

“I am not participating in this.”

“You already did.”

Snape closed his eyes.

I went.

His office was darker than the classroom and more damaged. One wall had been repaired with mismatched stone. Books crowded every surface, some in neat stacks and some piled as though they had been rescued in a hurry. A narrow camp bed stood folded behind the desk.

The sight of it bothered me.

Not because he had slept in the office. Because the bed looked practiced.

Like retreat had become furniture.

I found the salve beside a basin, unlabeled.

Of course it was unlabeled.

When I returned, Snape looked offended by my continued existence.

Pomfrey uncorked the jar, smelled it, and softened by a fraction.

“This is good.”

“I am touched by your surprise.”

“I am surprised you made something for yourself.”

The remark landed harder than she intended.

Snape's face went blank.

Pomfrey seemed to realize it. Her tone changed.

“Twice a day. And you are not to stand for more than an hour at a time. Your nerves are still healing.”

“They are aware.”

“I mean it.”

“So do they.”

She turned to me. “If he ignores me, send for Minerva.”

“I am not his keeper.”

“Thank you,” Snape said coldly.

“I am his colleague,” I continued. “Which means I can tell him he's being an idiot directly.”

Pomfrey smiled.

Snape looked betrayed by the universe.

After she left, he did not speak for several minutes.

I resumed inventory.

At last he said, “You have exceeded the scope of your contract.”

“By noticing a jar?”

“By appointing yourself commentator on my health.”

“I didn't.”

“You informed Pomfrey—”

“That you weren't using her salve. Which was true.”

“I was using another.”

“Which I also told her.”

His nostrils flared.

I set down my quill.

“If you want a rule, make one.”

He stared at me.

“A rule.”

“For working together. You clearly need them.”

“I need nothing of the sort.”

“You have spent twenty years controlling classrooms, hiding information from two opposing armies, and organizing a laboratory where pickled organs are shelved by properties only you understand. You absolutely need rules.”

His eyes went dangerously quiet.

I had learned enough by then to know that anger was not always the most dangerous thing in Snape's face.

“Very well,” he said. “Rule one. You do not discuss my medical condition with anyone unless I am unconscious, actively dying, or on fire.”

“What if you're unconscious and on fire?”

“Then I shall make every effort to wake up and extinguish myself before you become involved.”

I picked up my clipboard.

“Fine. My rule one: if your condition affects laboratory safety, it becomes my business while we're working.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

“Then we need separate labs.”

His gaze flicked to the ruined room around us.

We both knew there was only one safe workspace left.

“Fine,” he said as if the word were poisonous.

I wrote it down.

“Rule two,” he continued. “You do not enter my office without permission.”

“I was sent there by a healer.”

“Whom you encouraged.”

“Fine. My rule two: if you want me to respect privacy, say something is private before leaving it in the communal work area.”

“That is obvious.”

“Yesterday you threatened to hex me for opening a drawer marked stirring rods.”

“It did not contain stirring rods.”

“It contained stirring rods and one photograph.”

His face changed.

I regretted the words immediately.

I had seen only a corner before he shut the drawer: red hair, sunlight, the edge of a child's sleeve.

I had not needed a name.

“I didn't look,” I said.

“You saw enough.”

“I saw color.”

“Do not patronize me.”

“I'm not.”

“Then do not pretend ignorance.”

I took a slow breath.

“All right. I know who the photograph probably showed. I also know it's none of my business.”

His jaw tightened.

“And you expect gratitude for restraint?”

“No.”

“What, then?”

“Nothing.”

That stopped him.

I set the clipboard on the table between us.

“This is what I mean. I don't need payment every time I don't hurt you.”

His expression went cold enough to frost glass.

“That is an interesting choice of words.”

“It was deliberate.”

“You know nothing about me.”

“I know enough to notice you expect every kindness to come with an invoice.”

His wand was in his hand before I saw him move.

Not pointed at me.

Just there.

A habit. A warning. A wall.

I stayed still.

“Do not,” he said softly, “confuse observation with understanding.”

“I won't.”

The wand lowered by an inch.

“And don't confuse privacy with punishment,” I said.

His eyes flashed.

I thought I had gone too far.

Then he put the wand away.

“Rule three,” he said.

I waited.

“No amateur psychology before noon.”

I laughed.

He sat back, one hand touching his throat as though the exchange had cost him more than he wanted me to know.

“My rule three,” I said, “no threatening me with a wand because I annoy you.”

“I did not threaten you.”

“You held a wand during an argument.”

“I hold a wand while grading essays.”

“That explains a great deal about your students.”

His mouth twitched despite himself.

We added more rules.

No touching without warning unless someone was falling.

No opening sealed personal boxes.

No hiding cursed materials to avoid Ministry seizure without telling the other person first.

That one earned me a long stare.

No skipping meals during active brewing.

That one earned him the same.

No asking questions about the war if the answer was not relevant to the audit.

No lying when a direct answer was necessary for safety.

By the time we finished, there were twelve rules written in my handwriting and three amendments in his.

He objected to my use of the word “reasonable” in the heading.

I refused to change it.

At noon, we tested the fifth hidden phial.

It contained a soporific base with a deliberate error in the catalyst.

“Another failure,” I said.

“Another success,” Snape corrected.

I looked at him.

The distinction mattered.

So I crossed out FAILURE on the form and wrote SABOTAGED AS INTENDED.

He read it.

His eyes remained on the words for a long moment.

“Accurate,” he said quietly.

It was the first time he had praised my paperwork without making it sound like an insult.

I did not write it on the list.

Some things, I was learning, did not need to become evidence.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
